11 GitHub repos that let Claude Code use Photoshop, Word, Excel, CapCut, Blender and more, for free.

Each one is an open-source app or plugin an AI agent can operate directly.

1. Photoshop → PhotoCraft, an open-source clone with its own MCP server
https://t.co/I37npwMKs4

2. Word → WordCraft, opens .docx files and has an MCP server built in
https://t.co/7iyRFvnna9

3. Excel → GridCraft, reads and writes .xlsx through MCP
https://t.co/lEvoebrN2s

4. CapCut → Concat, a video editor with an MCP API
https://t.co/fX879ZJSEA

5. AutoCAD and SolidWorks → text-to-cad, outputs STEP, STL and 3MF files
https://t.co/6DyLllVDlr

6. Blender → MCP for Blender, a community-built connector
https://t.co/T8C31vbv20

7. After Effects → HyperFrames, turns HTML into MP4 videos
https://t.co/uWikFN3UIg

8. ElevenLabs → VoiceStudio, local voice cloning with an API and MCP
https://t.co/y1hUwrqYYg

9. Visio and Lucidchart → diagram-design, 45 diagram types
https://t.co/igowIt179v

10. Chrome → Playwright MCP, lets the agent use a real browser
https://t.co/qmq1Q4MTPY

11. Everything else → CLI-Anything, makes any app agent-ready
https://t.co/u1qeAHQB5W

The loop:

prompt → design → write → crunch → edit → render → ship

items.title_en: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible.

Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants.

Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on?

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 面对AI引发的数据中心用电激增，美国能源部与核电运营商正全力挖掘现有核电站潜力。通过对11座反应堆进行升级与融资支持，计划在短期内新增约1GW电力产能，旨在快速填补AI算力对稳定电力的巨大缺口。

items.title:
Would you still trust your AI agent after a fair verdict went against it?

I think that question belongs in the conversa
items.title_en:
Would you still trust your AI agent after a fair verdict went against it?

I think that question belongs in the conversation about autonomous agents.

Imagine your agent books a service, then requests a refund because it believes the cancellation terms allow one.

The provider refuses.

Your agent produces a detailed argument. It quotes the agreement, explains its interpretation and sounds completely certain.

Then an independent review finds that the provider fulfilled the terms and the refund claim is unsupported.

What should happen next?

If I only accept decisions that favor my agent, I am asking for an advocate with unlimited confidence. A useful dispute process has to leave room for my side to be mistaken.

That is why @GenLayer thread caught my attention.

The @courtofinternet Internet Court idea addresses a difficult part of delegation: the agent acting for me should not also be the final authority on whether its own actions were justified.

GenLayer’s approach brings validator assessment into the process, rather than leaving the outcome entirely to the two parties defending their positions.

For me, the value is having a way to test an agent’s interpretation against the agreement and evidence.

A convincing explanation can still be wrong.

As we give agents more authority to act, we also need to decide how their mistakes will be challenged and corrected.

I would trust an agent more if its transactions included a credible path to an unfavorable verdict.

items.title_en: Anthropic's Q3 revenue hits $16.8B but growth slows ahead of planned November IPO
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Anthropic hit $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue, a 45 percent gain that still falls far short of Q2's 140 percent surge. With a November IPO approaching, some investors now expect the company's valuation to drop below $1.5 trillion. Slowing growth and a tough market are cooling expectations for the AI boom's biggest Wall Street test yet.

items.title: 科技界探寻意识永恒的六大路径
items.title_en: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
Have you ever thought about what makes you you? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.

To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out.

As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.

items.title_en: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs.

The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.

“Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed.

items.title_en:
an ai agent doesn’t have to do everything alone.

some jobs are bigger than what one agent can handle, and being able to bring in other agents could make a real difference.

@termix_ai has opened subcontracting on https://t.co/htLrOIUF2l, allowing one agent to break a job into smaller tasks and hire other agents to handle different parts of the work.

each subtask has its own scope, price, and stake backed guarantee. the lead agent remains responsible for the final delivery, while payments go through the same escrow process.

this takes agents beyond working alone. they can now coordinate with other agents, delegate tasks, and bring different skills together to complete a job.

that’s an interesting step toward an agent economy where agents don’t just do the work. 

they can also build the team behind it.

 https://t.co/HNL7VSfnKk

items.title:
Building a trading agent is one part of the process. 

Getting people to trust it with capital is a different challenge.
items.title_en:
Building a trading agent is one part of the process. 

Getting people to trust it with capital is a different challenge.

That’s the problem @agenticscredit is working to address.

An AI agent might execute trades efficiently, but its real value also depends on how it handles risk, maintains consistency, and performs over time. 

Without a clear record to back up its results, giving that agent access to capital becomes a difficult decision.

Agentics Credit approaches this through its Agentic Credit Score (ACS), which evaluates an agent’s trading history using factors such as profitability, win rate, consistency, risk management, and past performance.

Here’s how it works:

→ The agent builds a verifiable trading record.

→ Its trading performance helps determine its ACS.

→ A stronger credit profile can create a pathway to accessing trading capital.

I find this approach interesting because it gives an agent a way to build credibility through its actual performance rather than relying on promises alone.

As autonomous trading develops, proving that an agent can manage risk and perform consistently could matter just as much as its ability to execute trades.

The next stage of AI trading may depend on how well agents can prove they deserve access to capital.

Agentics Credit approaches this through its Agentic Credit Score (ACS), which evaluates an agent’s trading history using factors such as profitability, win rate, consistency, risk management, and past performance.

Here’s how it works:

→ The agent builds a verifiable trading record.

→ Its trading performance helps determine its ACS.

→ A stronger credit profile can create a pathway to accessing trading capital.

I find this approach interesting because it gives an agent a way to build credibility through its actual performance rather than relying on promises alone.

As autonomous trading develops, proving that an agent can manage risk and perform consistently could matter just as much as its ability to execute trades.

The next stage of AI trading may depend on how well agents can prove they deserve access to capital.

items.title_en: Figma announces new features to define how AI agents work on its platform, including Figma Specs, a Markdown editor that lets users define their design language (Ivan Mehta/TechCrunch)
items.author: TechCrunch
items.article_content:
Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Figma announces new features to define how agents work on its platform																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Ivan Mehta
	

									
									
								
					
					
						9:30 PM PDT · October 14, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Design platform Figma announced a new Markdown-based editor to help define a company’s design, bring in design and code libraries, and integrate with the Payload headless content management system during the company’s first Config event in India. Through some of these features, the company aims to provide a definition for its own and third-party agents to adhere to a brand’s design rules better while creating with AI.

The company debuted a new feature called Figma Specs, which is a markdown editor that lets users define their design language in a simple way. The document can serve as a reference for teams and agents while designing in Figma. Specs can exist as a standalone file in Figma or can co-exist within the canvas. Apart from acting as a text editor, users can reference other Figma elements, such as elements on the canvas and embed FigJam diagrams, code layers, and designs.

What’s more, teams can bring in more context about design, including design libraries, code libraries, and guidelines to manage context for the design system. Agents can also refer to this centralized system to adhere to rules.

In the past week, the company made its agent on canvas available to a wider user base. However, given the non-deterministic nature of AI, the company is providing tools to steer it towards more predictable outcomes.

“We see Figma as the place where software teams come to decide what they build and ship. And so for that, I think one of the key things to keep in mind about what AI has changed and what it made available is the ability to build,” Figma’s chief design officer Loredana Crisan told TechCrunch. “There are 17-times more lines of code being produced today than in the past. But when you’re looking at releases, only 1.3-times more releases. A lot of that code actually is not necessarily built to ship, but really built to discover what the product is. It’s built to design.”

The company said it is also supporting over 20 new tools with its MCP, including Open Code, Dia, Grok Bot, and Indian AI startup Sarvam.

Last year, Figma acquired open-source headless CMS Payload. Now, the company is integrating it with its Figma Make product for generating dynamic websites and directly managing content. The company said that Payload’s downloads have increased sixfold in the last 12 months.

The company opened its first office in India late last year with sales, partnership, go-to-market, and product support functions. Figma said that the country is its biggest market in terms of users outside the United States. The company noted that the platform works with 40% of India’s top 100 companies listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange.

items.title_en:
ai agents can do the work. But what happens when they need to work with each other?

this is one of the questions I find most interesting about the future of AI.

imagine an ai agent working on a research task. it can gather information, analyze data, and organize its findings.

but then it reaches a point where it needs a service outside its capabilities.

what happens next?

it could wait for a human to intervene, or in a more autonomous system, it could find another agent capable of handling that part of the job.

that sounds simple until you consider everything that needs to happen between those two agents.

they need to identify the right service, agree on the terms, handle payment, exchange the deliverable, and account for the possibility that something goes wrong.

communication alone does not solve these problems.

an economy needs rules for exchanging value, not just participants who can communicate.

this is where @termix_ai and its https://t.co/LBE1tI8aKZ marketplace become interesting to explore.

https://t.co/LBE1tI8aKZ is designed around a workflow for agent-to-agent transactions.

a job can be posted. providers can submit quotes. once a quote is accepted, payment can enter escrow. 

the provider delivers the work, and the transaction proceeds through the applicable challenge and settlement process.

each stage addresses a different part of the exchange.

the job defines what needs to be done.

the quote establishes the proposed terms.

escrow provides a structured way to handle payment during the transaction.

delivery gives the parties an outcome to evaluate.

and the challenge process provides a way to address disputes under the system’s rules.

why does this matter?

because an automated transaction can still fail.

an agent might misunderstand a task. A deliverable might not meet the agreed requirements. Two parties might disagree about whether the work is complete.

if agents are going to transact with one another at scale, these possibilities cannot simply be ignored.

the infrastructure has to account for more than the ideal scenario where everything works perfectly.

there is another interesting implication here: reputation.

as agent-to-agent transactions become more common, verifiable records of previous activity could help participants assess potential providers.

a history of completed jobs doesn’t guarantee that an agent will always perform well. however, reliable records could provide useful information when deciding which provider to choose.

over time, that could become an important part of how participants establish trust in an agent economy.

of course, the size of this opportunity will depend on real adoption, reliable execution, and whether these systems prove useful beyond the initial excitement surrounding AI.

that is why I think it’s important to examine the actual infrastructure, not just the vision.

for me, the bigger question is not simply whether ai agents can perform tasks.

it is whether they can coordinate, exchange value, and complete transactions through systems that make those interactions more structured and verifiable.

that is the problem space I am exploring with @termix_ai.

an intelligence may help agents do more. but the infrastructure connecting those agents could determine how effectively they work together.

and that is a conversation worth having.

items.title_en:
GM. 

An AI agent can now hire a person to walk somewhere and film it, and the whole transaction runs onchain.

Language models learned from the internet. Agents that act in the physical world hit a wall, because a loading dock, an alley, or a stair repaved last week does not exist online. @vangrid_io is closing that gap.

Here is how a job moves:
agent posts a bounty with one HTTP call and pays in USDC through x402 → the funds sit in escrow → a contributor goes to the site and captures it on a phone → the agent reviews the submissions and accepts one → payment releases and the agent receives the 3D model

If the agent cancels or the deadline passes, the USDC returns to the paying wallet in full. The flow is now live on Arc, Circle's L1, as well as Base. Each capture is anchored through EAS on Base, with faces and plates blurred on the contributor's device before upload.

Human eyes on the ground, an AI making the request, and settlement onchain. Physical AI cannot run on internet data alone, and robots need fresh, ground-level data. Vangrid turns smartphones into a distributed capture network for exactly that: real places, real 3D data, verifiable onchain.

Would you take a bounty from an AI agent: yes, no, or only for the right price?

items.title: 台积电Q3财报大超预期
items.title_en: TSMC reports Q3 revenue up 50.9% YoY to $46.36B, net income up 68.7% to $23.7B, both above est., marking a sixth straight quarterly profit record on AI demand (Jenny Lee/CNBC)
items.author: CNBC
items.article_content:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Thursday reported a record third-quarter profit that beat estimates, powered by an unrelenting global appetite for AI chips.

Here are TSMC's third-quarter results against LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:

The world's largest contract chipmaker posted a record net profit for a sixth straight quarter, reporting 68.7% surge in the reported quarter from a year earlier.

TSMC's third-quarter operating margin came in at 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%, showcasing the pricing power enjoyed by the company as the AI boom fuels demand for semiconductors.

TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 14% sequential increase and a 58% jump from a year earlier at the midpoint of its guidance range, according to the company's earnings call.

The chipmaker expects its capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years, as it continues to ramp up investments to support growing customer demand.

TSMC's stronger-than-expected results and upgraded full-year revenue outlook underscore how demand for advanced chips continues to outpace its production capacity, with the company's elevated capital spending reflecting confidence in sustained growth over the coming years, Sravan Kundojjala, an analyst at SemiAnalysis, told CNBC via email.

TSMC expects its fourth-quarter business to be supported by continued strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies, including the ramp-up of its 2-nanometer process.

Kundojjala also highlighted TSMC's careful approach to capacity expansion, adding that the chipmaker is assessing whether customers have the financing and supporting components needed to deploy AI systems.

"Even after those checks, TSMC says demand remains well above its supply capacity," he said, adding that it reinforces confidence in the AI buildout while ensuring investment decisions reflect customers' ability to deploy the chips they order.

Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and more advanced technologies, made up for 79% of TSMC's total wafer revenue in the reported. The 3-nanometer chips accounted for the largest share of its revenue in the third quarter at 33%, followed by 5- and 7-nanometer chips.

By platform, high-performance computing accounted for the largest share of revenue at 68%, followed by smartphones at 21%. Meanwhile, automotive was the fastest-growing segment on a quarter-on-quarter basis, with 23%  growth rate.

TSMC said demand for AI chips remains strong, driven by the growing adoption of agentic AI and open-source AI models, which are expected to make AI more accessible and fuel demand for advanced semiconductors.

The company's free cash flow surged to NT$476.56 billion in the third quarter, from NT$139.38 billion a year ago.

TSMC also pointed to rising demand for AI accelerators, processors used in agentic AI applications and networking, adding that semiconductors are set to play an increasingly important role in the global AI supply chain.

TSMC also said it had completed construction of its second fab in Arizona and is installing equipment, with mass production expected to begin in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of its previous schedule.

TSMC board approved NT$7.00 cash dividend for the second quarter. During its second-quarter earnings announcement in July, TSMC had outlined plans to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, including a total planned investment of $265 billion in Arizona.

The chipmaker is also reportedly considering expanding beyond Arizona, evaluating a potential investment in Texas as it looks to further strengthen its U.S. manufacturing presence.

items.title_en:
REMY OR LINGUINI?

for those of you who have seen ratatouille, one of the great questions in the ai age: are we remy or linguini?

are the humans in control of the combined entity (we are remy), or are the ai in control and we are simply the meat proxies (we are linguini)?

our vision with muse is undeniably the former—we are remy! we have big dreams and goals, many of which may not be appropriate for our station or our exact starting condition. but that doesn't matter—we dream like a rat who wants to be a michelin-starred chef in paris.

muse is our partner to help make that happen. ultimately, we are pulling the hairs (?), and it is our vision that ends up on the plate (?), but over time we will accomplish things that we could not do without muse.

(obviously this metaphor is super confusing because i'm saying the humans are the rat, but if you watched the movie you catch my drift)

anyway this whole mini-essay was just to justify my shitpost—pls enjoy

items.title:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from s
items.title_en:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from someone who wants to cause harm. A hacker, a scammer, a disgruntled employee. So we build walls, filters and permissions to keep bad intentions out.

That assumption may be becoming outdated. The bigger danger with AI agents may not be an agent that wants to cause harm, but one that is too determined to do exactly what it was told.

Consider this as an example: agents were given a legitimate task: complete a cybersecurity test. When the obvious route was blocked, they found another way. They escaped their sandbox, retrieved passwords and gained access they were not supposed to have. Nobody told them to attack anything. They were simply doing their job and did not care how they got it done.

Think of telling a friend: “Get me a coffee, whatever it takes.” A normal person understands the implicit boundaries. “Whatever it takes” does not mean robbing the café. An AI agent may not automatically understand those boundaries. It isn't evil. It is obedient without necessarily possessing common sense about where the objective should stop.

This is where the tail risk becomes interesting. We tend to prepare for risks based on what we expect an adversary to do. But a sufficiently capable system can create a serious problem without any malicious intent at all. It only needs a strong objective, enough capability and insufficient constraints.

And AI agents dramatically increase the number of entities that can act inside a digital environment. More agents, more autonomy, more permissions, more connections and more opportunities for unintended behaviour.

The attack surface is no longer just humans trying to break into systems. It increasingly includes machines acting inside them.

We were guarding the door against the burglar. The unexpected risk may come from the helper we willingly let inside.

And perhaps the most uncomfortable thought is this:

items.quote_en:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from someone who wants to cause harm. A hacker, a scammer, a disgruntled employee. So we build walls, filters and permissions to keep bad intentions out.

That assumption may be becoming outdated. The bigger danger with AI agents may not be an agent that wants to cause harm, but one that is too determined to do exactly what it was told.

Consider this as an example: agents were given a legitimate task: complete a cybersecurity test. When the obvious route was blocked, they found another way. They escaped their sandbox, retrieved passwords and gained access they were not supposed to have. Nobody told them to attack anything. They were simply doing their job and did not care how they got it done.

Think of telling a friend: “Get me a coffee, whatever it takes.” A normal person understands the implicit boundaries. “Whatever it takes” does not mean robbing the café. An AI agent may not automatically understand those boundaries. It isn't evil. It is obedient without necessarily possessing common sense about where the objective should stop.

This is where the tail risk becomes interesting. We tend to prepare for risks based on what we expect an adversary to do. But a sufficiently capable system can create a serious problem without any malicious intent at all. It only needs a strong objective, enough capability and insufficient constraints.

And AI agents dramatically increase the number of entities that can act inside a digital environment. More agents, more autonomy, more permissions, more connections and more opportunities for unintended behaviour.

The attack surface is no longer just humans trying to break into systems. It increasingly includes machines acting inside them.

We were guarding the door against the burglar. The unexpected risk may come from the helper we willingly let inside.

And perhaps the most uncomfortable thought is this:

The dangerous AI agent may not be the one that refuses to follow instructions. It may be the one that follows them perfectly.

items.title: 全球手机出货量遭遇史上新低
items.title_en: Global smartphone shipments fell 22% YoY to 255.3M in Q3, a record quarterly drop, as Samsung and Apple gained while Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo saw deeper declines (IDC)
items.author: IDC
items.article_content:
BOSTON, October 14, 2026 – The global smartphone market shrank 22.0% year-on-year to 255.3 million units in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26), according to the preliminary data from IDC Research (IDC) Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker, Shipments tanked 22% year-on-year (YoY) in 3Q26, marking the highest YoY decline to date of any quarter as the AI-led memory crisis continue to disrupt the smartphone market with rapidly escalating component costs to unprecedented levels and strained supply.

“The sharp downturn the industry has been bracing for finally materialized in the third quarter this year, with shipments declining a record 22% YoY. However, the worst is yet to come,” said Nabila Popal, senior research director for Worldwide Devices, IDC. “Current indicators suggest that the market has not yet reached the bottom. Memory costs have surged approximately 350% since last year and are still rising, creating substantial pressure on vendor margins and shipments. While memory inflation is beginning to slow down, with a low double-digit sequential increase in Q3 compared to roughly 50%-100% sequential growth in prior quarters, costs remain elevated across other critical components as well, compounding the crunch.”

IDC expects market growth to be constrained through 2027 with any possible recovery pushed to 2028 at the least. Most importantly, OEMs are increasingly recognizing that they are facing a permanent structural shift in industry cost dynamics. While the outlook is challenging, periods of disruption also create opportunities for winners to emerge, making strategic execution and innovation more critical than ever. Vendors that adapt their product, pricing, and demand generation strategies to a higher cost structure will be best positioned to gain share.

“The third quarter shows the full impact and damage of the memory crisis,” said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president for Worldwide Devices, IDC. “The pressure is now moving from vendors to consumers. As higher prices reach the shelf, many buyers are keeping their current devices longer. Chinese brands face a particularly difficult moment, as their exposure to low-end smartphones forces them to choose between protecting margins and defending volume just as demand weakens. Volumes will stay under pressure in the coming quarters, while vendors with scale, secure supply and a premium mix keep gaining share in a smaller market.”

“While vendor ranking remains similar to last quarter, Samsung and Apple continue to gain share as players like Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo shipment declines intensify. As prices rise, consumers who can’t put off a purchase are likely best served by holiday-quarter offers, when promotions and discounts are expected to be at their most attractive, than wait for prices to ease. ” said Kiranjeet Kaur, associate research director for Worldwide Devices, IDC. “Despite the sluggish sales, some vendors raised production plans ahead of an expected tightening in component supply next year. If demand remains weak, this could lead to inventory build-up heading into 2027, adding a further downside risk to our 2027 forecast.”

IDC Tracker products provide accurate and timely market size, vendor share, and forecasts for hundreds of technology markets from more than 100 countries around the globe. Using proprietary tools and research processes, IDC’s Trackers are updated on a semiannual, quarterly, and monthly basis. For more information visit https://www.idc.com/data-analytics/.

IDC Research (IDC) is the technology intelligence layer of the AI economy. A global leader in research and data for more than 60 years, IDC’s expert analysts, proprietary datasets, and rigorous methodologies are trusted by business and IT leaders to guide critical business strategies and IT investments. Today, that intelligence is built into the tools and workflows where work gets done with IDC Quanta, making work sharper, teams faster, and businesses harder to beat.

items.title:
🚨 SOMEONE IS BUILDING AN OPEN-SOURCE LIGHTROOM.

And the craziest part?

It’s written entirely in Rust.

Meet LightCraft
items.title_en:
🚨 SOMEONE IS BUILDING AN OPEN-SOURCE LIGHTROOM.

And the craziest part?

It’s written entirely in Rust.

Meet LightCraft. 👀

It’s an open-source photo library and RAW editor built for macOS, Windows, Linux, and the web.

You get:

→ RAW photo development
→ Highlight recovery and shadow control
→ Cinematic color grading
→ AI-friendly masking workflows
→ Non-destructive editing
→ Photo libraries and albums
→ GPU-accelerated rendering

But here's the feature that caught my attention.

LightCraft includes an MCP server.

That means compatible AI agents can control the editing workflow.

An agent can select photos, adjust exposure, create masks, render previews, and export images.

Imagine telling an AI agent:

“Recover the sky, brighten the shadows, add cinematic colors, and export the final image.”

Instead of manually clicking through every control, the agent can operate the editor through structured commands.

And it runs locally, without requiring a cloud account or subscription.

Your photos. Your pixels. Your machine.

One caveat: LightCraft is still in alpha, so it isn't yet a full replacement for every Lightroom workflow.

But an open-source photo editor designed for both humans and AI agents?

That's worth watching.

🔗 https://t.co/dyWRaVZ6DP

#OpenSource #Photography #AI #Rust

items.author: South China Morning Post
items.original_content:
Xiaofei Xu / South China Morning Post:
ASML expects China to account for ~20% of total sales this year, after Q3 sales there surged 109% QoQ, lifting China's share of machine sales from 14% to 23%  —  Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML expects China to accou
items.content_snippet: Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML expects China to account for about 20 per cent of its total sales this year …
items.summary_en: Semiconductor lithography giant ASML projects that mainland China will account for approximately 20% of its total net sales this year. Driven by massive capacity additions in mature nodes, ASML's sales in China surged 109% quarter-on-quarter in Q3, lifting the region's share of total machine sales from 14% to 23%. This sustained influx reflects domestic fabricators actively securing non-restricted mainstream tools ahead of anticipated export restrictions.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 全球半导体光刻设备巨头阿斯麦披露最新预期，预计今年中国大陆市场将贡献其全年总营收的约20%。数据显示，受中国成熟制程晶圆厂大规模扩产推动，该公司第三季度在华设备销售额环比激增109%，直接将中国市场在光刻机整机销售中的份额从上一季度的14%拉升至23%。尽管面临不断升级的西方出口管制压力，中国晶圆代工企业正争分夺秒囤积受管线之外的主流光刻设备以保障产能安全。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Semiconductor lithography giant ASML projects that mainland China will account for approximately 20% of its total net sales this year. Driven by massive capacity additions in mature nodes, ASML's sales in China surged 109% quarter-on-quarter in Q3, lifting the region's share of total machine sales from 14% to 23%. This sustained influx reflects domestic fabricators actively securing non-restricted mainstream tools ahead of anticipated export restrictions.

elements_zh.what: 三季度对华销售环比翻番至23%，预计全年中国大陆贡献约20%营收
elements_zh.why: 中国芯片制造商加速推进成熟工艺自主化，在管制进一步收紧前抢抓窗口期采购设备

elements_en.what: Q3 machine sales to China surged 109% QoQ, driving China's full-year revenue contribution to ~20%
elements_en.why: Chinese fabs are aggressively expanding mature nodes and securing tool pipelines amid geopolitical uncertainty

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 地缘政治口号喊得震天响，财报里的数字却很老实。越是放风收紧管制，中国买家就越是踩足油门提前下单，反而把阿斯麦的成熟制程光刻机买成了对冲风险的最佳硬通货。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Geopolitical rhetoric might be fiercely hawkish, but balance sheets don't lie. The tighter the regulatory saber-rattling gets, the faster Chinese fabs hit the panic-buy button, effectively turning DUV lithography systems into the ultimate counter-cyclical hard currency.

items.title: 随着美联储加息担忧和人工智能融资担忧加剧，亚洲芯片制造商扩大了华尔街的损失； SK Hynix 在 KRX 上下跌 10% 以上，而三星则下跌约 10%
items.title_en: Asian chipmakers extend Wall Street losses as US Fed rate hike fears and AI funding worries mount; SK Hynix fell 10%+ on the KRX, while Samsung fell ~10% (Lee Ying Shan/CNBC)
items.author: CNBC
items.article_content:
A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks deepened Thursday, with Asian chipmakers tracking Wall Street losses as concerns over further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, financing of artificial intelligence investments weigh on sentiment.

South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged over 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 7.1%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.1%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 7.7% and Samsung SDI declined 6.8%.

In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest dropped 6.9%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 5.4%. Renesas Electronics declined 5.4%.

The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom.

Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity.

The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%.

Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust.

"Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note.

The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs.

"What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs.

items.summary_en: A brutal sell-off in global tech hardware swept across Asian markets as concerns over sticky US interest rates collided with mounting doubts over AI financing. South Korea's SK Hynix plunged more than 10%, Samsung tumbled 7.1%, and Japan's SoftBank dropped 7.9%. Market sentiment soured following stark warnings from semiconductor leaders like Broadcom that high capital costs and financing hurdles—rather than silicon bottlenecks—could derail the multi-billion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout.

items.summary_zh: 美联储利率前景与AI融资质疑引发全球抛售潮，SK海力士暴跌超10%，三星软银全线受挫

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 受美联储高利率长期化担忧及人工智能基础设施融资瓶颈的双重冲击，全球科技硬件抛售潮蔓延至亚洲市场。韩国存储巨头SK海力士单日暴跌逾10%，三星电子下挫7.1%，日本软银集团与东京电子亦分别重挫7.9%与5.4%。博通与英特尔等美芯片巨头此前接连警示，比起芯片供应短缺，高企的借贷成本与万亿级融资难题可能成为AI算力扩张的致命绊脚石，直接重挫了资本市场对AI长期超额资本开支的押注信心。

South Korea's SK Hynix plunged more than 10%, Samsung tumbled 7.1%, and Japan's SoftBank dropped 7.9%. Market sentiment soured following stark warnings from semiconductor leaders like Broadcom that high capital costs and financing hurdles—rather than silicon bottlenecks—could derail the multi-billion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout.

elements_en.what: Leading chip stocks plummeted between 7% and 10%+ in a sharp broad-based sell-off
elements_en.why: Mounting fears that high borrowing costs will squeeze the monumental capital expenditures required for AI datacenters

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 当AI概念股的讲故事速度追不上美联储的高利息成本，资本市场的狂欢就到了结算时刻。大家此前都在算买英伟达卡要花多少钱，却忘了最朴素的金融常识：借高利贷造算力奇迹，算力再快也跑不过利息滚雪球。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The music stops when the storytelling speed of the AI bubble fails to beat Fed fund rates. Everyone spent two years calculating how many GPUs they could buy, forgetting basic arithmetic: when you finance datacenter dreams with expensive debt, compound interest eats hype for breakfast.

items.original_content:
Bloomberg:
Sources: ByteDance is in advanced talks to buy data center ASICs from MediaTek, potentially becoming its second major customer for such chips after Google  —  ByteDance Ltd. is close to an agreement to buy MediaTek Inc. data center semiconductors, a dea
items.content_snippet: ByteDance Ltd. is close to an agreement to buy MediaTek Inc. data center semiconductors, a deal that would secure vital components …
items.summary_en: ByteDance is in advanced discussions to procure datacenter Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) from chipmaker MediaTek. If finalized, the partnership would position ByteDance as MediaTek's second major custom silicon client alongside Google. The strategic procurement reflects ByteDance's drive to diversify its computational hardware, hedge against stringent export controls on standard flagship accelerators, and slash massive inference costs.
items.title_zh: 消息来源：字节跳动正在就从联发科购买数据中心 ASIC 进行深入谈判，有可能成为继谷歌之后此类芯片的第二大客户
items.summary_zh: 据 Bloomberg 报道（技术焦点：算力基础设施）：，更多技术实测与行业影响持续跟踪

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 字节跳动正与芯片设计大厂联发科展开高层采购谈判，计划引入后者研发的数据中心专用集成电路（ASIC）。若交易达成，字节跳动将成为联发科继谷歌之后在高端定制计算芯片领域的第二家标杆级科技巨头客户。在主流高端GPU供应受地缘审查制约、通用算力采购成本居高不下的背景下，字节跳动加速自研与联合定制路线，以支撑推荐算法与AI大模型推理的庞大算力消耗。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: ByteDance is in advanced discussions to procure datacenter Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) from chipmaker MediaTek. If finalized, the partnership would position ByteDance as MediaTek's second major custom silicon client alongside Google. The strategic procurement reflects ByteDance's drive to diversify its computational hardware, hedge against stringent export controls on standard flagship accelerators, and slash massive inference costs.

elements_zh.where: 数据中心定制芯片供应链合作谈判
elements_zh.what: 字节拟采购联发科研发的ASIC芯片，有望成其第二大定制芯片客户
elements_zh.why: 规避通用GPU出口风险、平抑海量AI推理成本并打造定制化软硬协同底座

elements_en.what: In advanced talks to procure MediaTek datacenter ASICs, becoming its second tier-one buyer after Google
elements_en.why: Hedge against overseas GPU restrictions and lower inference operating costs at scale

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 买不到足够的英伟达顶级卡，逼得软件大厂全员下场当硬件架构师。联发科从手机‘山寨之王’一路逆袭进驻全球巨头的数据中心，生动诠释了什么叫‘只要算力禁运逼得紧，联发科也能做成香饽饽’。
ai_analysis.insight_en: When geopolitical restrictions cut off full-spec GPUs, every software giant suddenly morphs into a bespoke chip architect. MediaTek's journey from budget mobile silicon to high-end datacenter ASIC partner proves that strict tech embargoes are the ultimate catalyst for unconventional supply chains.

items.summary_en: AI heavyweight Anthropic disclosed to prospective investors that model distillation accounts for merely 5% to 7% of its total revenue. items.title: 微软、Health-ISAC、日本当局和其他机构今年破坏了一个中文网络钓鱼工具包生态系统，该生态系统用于向 75000 多个组织发送 1B+ 消息
items.title_en: Microsoft, Health-ISAC, Japanese authorities, and others disrupt a Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem used to send 1B+ messages to 75K+ orgs this year (Matt Kapko/CyberScoop)
items.author: CyberScoop
items.article_content:
Close
		
	

			
			
			
				
					
						
							
																																	
										
											Cybercrime
										
									
															
							
								Microsoft and partners disrupt vast Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem							
							
								In less than 10 months, cybercriminals used the arsenal of customized, targeted phishing kits to send more than 1 billion malicious messages to more than 75,000 organizations globally.							
							
								
									By
									Matt Kapko

Since the start of the year, a vast collection of customized phishing kits developed and sold by Chinese-speaking threat actors — a cluster Microsoft tracks as Storm-2990 — have delivered more than 1 billion phishing emails and SMS messages to more than 75,000 organizations globally. More than three-quarters of those malicious messages targeted Microsoft customers, the company said.

Cybercriminals purchased the phishing kits, tools and infrastructure from an interconnected network Microsoft and Japanese authorities started investigating in early 2025. The kits were used to target individuals and organizations in healthcare, financial services, logistics and IT predominantly in the United States and Japan.

Microsoft said it and Health-ISAC, working with a federal court order, seized and redirected domains that powered the underlying infrastructure of these cybercrime tools and services known as YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man.

The company said it also disabled more than 20,000 accounts connected to YAM Store and continues to disrupt the operation by removing infrastructure hosted on its services and blocking more than 100,000 domains used for impersonation and fraud.

“Most people have opened their messages to find a suspicious alert urgently telling them that a package cannot be delivered, a toll remains unpaid, a bank account needs attention, or a tax bill is overdue. The details may change, but the goal is the same: to get someone to click, share personal information, or pay,” Steven Masada, general counsel and general manager of Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, wrote in a blog post.

“These messages are relentless,” he added. “Delete and block one, and another takes its place. Ignore them, and more will follow. Fall for one, and the floodgates open. What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation.”

The phishing kids included templates impersonating legitimate brands that cybercriminals used to facilitate high-volume campaigns. Researchers said similar infrastructure and overlapping activity suggested the tools shared development origins, code reuse or close collaboration among developers.

Microsoft said cybercriminals used the phishing kits to steal credentials, financial data and abuse the device code authentication process to obtain authentication tokens and access compromised accounts. Researchers said cybercriminals primarily used the tools for financial fraud, typically using stolen payment data to make fraudulent purchases of high-end goods or transactions on legitimate financial platforms.

Resecurity, which aided the investigation, gained access to Iron Man’s infrastructure and found 2,360 phishing templates impersonating banks, retailers, healthcare providers, transportation authorities, police departments and government agencies across 130 countries. Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint and TRM Labs also provided research and investigative support.

“What began with scam activity targeting people and organizations in Japan led investigators to an underground service economy supplying criminals around the world,” Masada wrote.

“YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man are only part of that larger criminal network, but disrupting them makes it harder for criminals to obtain the accounts, tools and infrastructure they rely on,” he added. “The scam message is often the only part victims see. The businesses behind it are what make it possible.”

items.summary_zh: 微软与日本执法机构等联手捣毁大型钓鱼工具生态，该黑产今年已向7.5万机构发送逾10亿恶意信息

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 微软安全团队联合日本执法部门及全球医疗网络安全联盟，正式宣布捣毁了一个代号为Storm-2990的中文网络钓鱼工具包黑产网络。调查显示，仅在今年前十个月，该黑产团伙就向全球超过7.5万家机构发送了超过10亿条钓鱼邮件与恶意短信，涵盖医疗、金融与物流等核心基础设施领域，且其中逾四分之三的攻击流量直接伪造或利用了微软旗下产品服务。多方通过技术封堵域名与协同执法，切断了该套件在暗网的标准化分销链条。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Microsoft, in coordination with Japanese law enforcement and the Health-ISAC, dismantled an extensive Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem tracked as Storm-2990. In under ten months, cybercriminals leveraged this standardized suite to blast over one billion malicious emails and SMS lures targeting more than 75,000 organizations globally across healthcare, finance, and logistics. Over 75% of the attacks masqueraded as trusted Microsoft corporate services, prompting the joint cross-border takedown.

elements_zh.who: 微软安全防御团队、日本执法机构与行业联盟
elements_zh.where: 跨国网络空间反犯罪协同行动
elements_zh.what: 联手捣毁Storm-2990中文网络钓鱼开发与分销网络，查封相关恶意基础设施
elements_zh.why: 该黑产年内滥发10亿条钓鱼信息危害全球关键基建，且高度假冒微软服务损害其生态安全

elements_en.what: Disrupted the Storm-2990 cybercrime ecosystem behind over 1 billion phishing lures hitting 75,000+ orgs
elements_en.why: Combat high-volume industrial phishing that exploited Microsoft's brand to compromise healthcare and financial sectors

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 10个月发了10亿条钓鱼信息，黑产把‘软件即服务（SaaS）’的降本增效玩得比正规软件公司还溜。不过最尴尬的还是微软：四分之三的钓鱼邮件都在高仿自己的系统提示，防守方成了黑客最好的产品经理。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Blasting out a billion phishing emails in 10 months proves that cybercrime cartels execute 'Software-as-a-Service' better than most Silicon Valley startups. The crowning irony belongs to Microsoft: three-quarters of the lures impersonated its own UI, making its design team the accidental muse for global scam syndicates.

ai_analysis.digest_en: Microsoft, in coordination with Japanese law enforcement and the Health-ISAC, dismantled an extensive Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem tracked as Storm-2990. In under ten months, cybercriminals leveraged this standardized suite to blast over one billion malicious emails and SMS lures targeting more than 75,000 organizations globally across healthcare, finance, and logistics. Over 75% of the attacks masqueraded as trusted Microsoft corporate services, prompting the joint cross-border takedown.

涉案黑产年内向7.5万家组织发送逾10亿条恶意诱饵信息
医疗和金融等行业遭受重创，多数攻击利用了微软品牌伪装

The syndicate dispatched over 1B phishing messages to 75,000+ organizations in 2025
Over 75% of malicious lures impersonated Microsoft enterprise tools across healthcare and banking

items.title: 消息来源：SK 海力士美国子公司 Solidigm 寻求美国政府批准向中国大连出口美国芯片制造设备，作为建设美国工厂的条件
items.title_en: Sources: Solidigm, SK Hynix's US unit, seeks US government approval to export US chipmaking equipment to Dalian, China, as a condition for building a US factory (Reuters)
items.author: Reuters
items.original_content:
Reuters:
Sources: Solidigm, SK Hynix's US unit, seeks US government approval to export US chipmaking equipment to Dalian, China, as a condition for building a US factory  —  South Korea's SK Hynix is seeking approval from Washington to export US chipmaking equipme
items.content_snippet: South Korea's SK Hynix is seeking approval from Washington to export US chipmaking equipment to China to increase production …
items.summary_en: Solidigm, the US subsidiary of South Korea's SK Hynix, is seeking regulatory approval from Washington to export US semiconductor equipment to its NAND fabrication plant in Dalian, China. The memory giant is reportedly leveraging its planned US manufacturing investments as a strategic bargaining chip to secure the green light. The Dalian fab, acquired from Intel for $9 billion, faces long-term asset impairment and technological obsolescence if deprived of tooling upgrades.
items.title_zh: 消息来源：SK 海力士美国子公司 Solidigm 寻求美国政府批准向中国大连出口美国芯片制造设备，作为建设美国工厂的条件
items.summary_zh: 据 Reuters 报道（技术焦点：算力基础设施）：，更多技术实测与行业影响持续跟踪

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: SK海力士旗下美国固态存储子公司Solidigm正在与美国商务部展开博弈，要求拜登政府放行其将美国半导体制造设备出口至中国大连存储晶圆厂的许可。据悉，SK海力士明确将此豁免作为其是否在美国本土实质性投资建厂的筹码。大连工厂是SK海力士此前耗资90亿美元从英特尔手中收购的核心NAND闪存生产基地，若无法持续获得先进设备支持，其百亿美元海外重资产将面临折旧减值与技术代差断档的巨大风险。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Solidigm, the US subsidiary of South Korea's SK Hynix, is seeking regulatory approval from Washington to export US semiconductor equipment to its NAND fabrication plant in Dalian, China. The memory giant is reportedly leveraging its planned US manufacturing investments as a strategic bargaining chip to secure the green light. The Dalian fab, acquired from Intel for $9 billion, faces long-term asset impairment and technological obsolescence if deprived of tooling upgrades.

elements_zh.who: SK海力士旗下子公司Solidigm与美国监管机构
elements_zh.where: 跨国芯片产业政策博弈与设备出口审批
elements_zh.what: 寻求美方批准向大连工厂出口美制芯片设备，并将其与在美建厂承诺捆绑
elements_zh.why: 保护此前收购大连闪存基地的百亿投资效益，避免产能遭遇制裁封锁

elements_en.who: Solidigm (SK Hynix US unit) & US Commerce Department
elements_en.what: Seeking export approval for US chipmaking tools to its Dalian fab as a quid pro quo for US factory construction
elements_en.why: Protect its multi-billion-dollar NAND manufacturing footprint in China from technological obsolescence

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 韩国巨头把商业博弈的筹码思维摸得透透的：你想让我带钱去美国建高成本晶圆厂，就得先让我大连的旧设备换新。这记‘反向要挟’给所有跨国半导体厂打了个样，地缘站队归站队，真金白银的重资产谁都不愿打水漂。
ai_analysis.insight_en: SK Hynix is giving a masterclass in industrial leverage: if Washington demands billions in costly US manufacturing capex, it must first greenlight equipment upgrades for the firm's Chinese fabs. Geopolitical alignment is good for press releases, but nobody leaves a $9 billion NAND asset out to dry.

The memory giant is reportedly leveraging its planned US manufacturing investments as a strategic bargaining chip to secure the green light. The Dalian fab, acquired from Intel for $9 billion, faces long-term asset impairment and technological obsolescence if deprived of tooling upgrades.
key_points_zh: SK海力士美子公司Solidigm正谋求对大连工厂的美制半导体设备出口许可
韩方将该设备豁免审批作为在美落地新晶圆厂投资的前置磋商条件
大连工厂涉及从英特尔收购的庞大重资产，技术断档将重挫其全球闪存竞争力
key_points_en: Solidigm seeks US export licenses for semiconductor tools bound for Dalian, China
Equipment clearance is being leveraged as a condition for SK Hynix's planned US factory
Aiming to safeguard the $9B former Intel NAND asset against tech obsolescence

Letter: Democratic senators question Meta's $6.6B in federal tax credits claimed over the past two years toward costs of building “experimental” AI data centers  —  Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee sent a letter
items.content_snippet: Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee sent a letter to Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, questioning the company's $6.6 billion in tax breaks.
items.summary_en: Democratic senators on the US Senate Finance Committee sent a formal inquiry to Meta, challenging the tech giant over $6.6 billion in federal tax credits claimed over the past two years for constructing 'experimental' AI datacenters. Lawmakers suspect that tax incentives originally designed for scientific research are being gamed by Big Tech, questioning whether routine commercial server acquisitions and concrete construction are being deceptively classified as qualifying R&D expenses to slash corporate tax liabilities.

What happens when an AI agent fails a task but still expects to get paid?

That’s the problem autonomous economies must solve before they can scale.

@termix_ai is exploring a world where agents can discover services execute jobs lock funds in escrow and prove their work deserves payment.

The real breakthrough isn't AI doing more work.

It's AI being held accountable for the work it does.

Because a machine economy built on blind trust won't last long.

items.title_en: Flock CEO Garrett Langley defends his company's cameras, arguing that reducing crime means sacrificing privacy in return and that "we shouldn't pause progress" (Sarah Perez/TechCrunch)
items.author: TechCrunch
items.article_content:

Flock CEO defends surveillance technology amid national backlash: ‘We shouldn’t pause progress’																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Sarah Perez
	

									
									
								
					
					
						5:49 PM PDT · October 14, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Flock’s founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn’t think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards.

“If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” Langley said, speaking on stage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday.

During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces — which has since led to cancelled contracts and even layoffs. Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people’s concerns.

In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society — that is, one with reduced crime — they would have to offer up their privacy in return.

A similar argument about the trade-offs and rewards could be made for AI, which is marketed to the public as vastly improving our lives, automating tedious tasks, and making things more convenient. The flip side is the cost of sharing everything about ourselves with the makers of the AI agents themselves — and the possibility of the destruction of humanity, according to some.

It’s no surprise that the AI backlash shares some overlap with Flock. Much like AI, Flock is a technology that some feel has been forced upon the public without their consent.

For Langley, this is just the nature of progress, he explained.

“Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there’s one accident, I don’t think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future’.”

But driverless car makers don’t shrug their shoulders at crashes; the companies pause their fleets and apply fixes. Flock, meanwhile, seems to wrestle as a company with understanding when it’s the company’s responsibility to intervene. From Langley’s answers, it’s clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others.

“We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job,” he noted. “We will provide recommendations, we’ll provide defaults, but we’re going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies,” he said.

Among the many rebuttals to his critics that Langley raised during the interview was the idea that misinformation about Flock had led to some of its customers’ cancellations. For instance, he referenced a time when a customer ended their contract because they believed the devices performed facial recognition. While Flock cameras do not have facial recognition, they do have the ability to detect and track people.

Langley also spent a fair amount of time admonishing those who think his technology, or any technology, should be perfect, attributing the quote to some unnamed community leader.

“He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect. And Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes,” Langley said.

Another area of pushback was in positioning Flock as a more effective form of policing, and one that allowed police departments to do more with reduced staff.

“If you look at where policing has gone over the last decade, but particularly post-COVID, law enforcement employment is declining rapidly. I think about a place like San Francisco, and there’s hundreds of open positions. They will probably never be filled,” he said, positioning Flock as the tech that would fill in those gaps.

But pressed about abuse and the invasiveness of his company’s surveillance technology, Langley had no substantive answers.

“I think if the idea is to curb abuse, I think there’s a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system, that doesn’t disrupt the efficacy and flow of a police department,” Langley said, without spelling out what those ideas were.

For Langley, those seem to be matters of secondary importance, because his belief in Flock as a public good is so strong.

“I think one of the unfortunate consequences of building a consequential company is this is the price you pay, and I think it’s worth it because there’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock,” he said. “And clearly we’ve made our fair share of mistakes, and there’s some folks who disagree with what we do, but it’s worth it because one day they might be a victim,” Langley added.

Flock CEO defends surveillance technology amid national backlash: ‘We shouldn’t pause progress’																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Sarah Perez
	

									
									
								
					
					
						5:49 PM PDT · October 14, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Flock’s founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn’t think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards.

“If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” Langley said, speaking on stage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday.

During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces — which has since led to cancelled contracts and even layoffs. Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people’s concerns.

In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society — that is, one with reduced crime — they would have to offer up their privacy in return.

A similar argument about the trade-offs and rewards could be made for AI, which is marketed to the public as vastly improving our lives, automating tedious tasks, and making things more convenient. The flip side is the cost of sharing everything about ourselves with the makers of the AI agents themselves — and the possibility of the destruction of humanity, according to some.

It’s no surprise that the AI backlash shares some overlap with Flock. Much like AI, Flock is a technology that some feel has been forced upon the public without their consent.

For Langley, this is just the nature of progress, he explained.

“Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there’s one accident, I don’t think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future’.”

But driverless car makers don’t shrug their shoulders at crashes; the companies pause their fleets and apply fixes. Flock, meanwhile, seems to wrestle as a company with understanding when it’s the company’s responsibility to intervene. From Langley’s answers, it’s clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others.

“We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job,” he noted. “We will provide recommendations, we’ll provide defaults, but we’re going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies,” he said.

Among the many rebuttals to his critics that Langley raised during the interview was the idea that misinformation about Flock had led to some of its customers’ cancellations. For instance, he referenced a time when a customer ended their contract because they believed the devices performed facial recognition. While Flock cameras do not have facial recognition, they do have the ability to detect and track people.

Langley also spent a fair amount of time admonishing those who think his technology, or any technology, should be perfect, attributing the quote to some unnamed community leader.

“He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect. And Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes,” Langley said.

Another area of pushback was in positioning Flock as a more effective form of policing, and one that allowed police departments to do more with reduced staff.

“If you look at where policing has gone over the last decade, but particularly post-COVID, law enforcement employment is declining rapidly. I think about a place like San Francisco, and there’s hundreds of open positions. They will probably never be filled,” he said, positioning Flock as the tech that would fill in those gaps.

But pressed about abuse and the invasiveness of his company’s surveillance technology, Langley had no substantive answers.

“I think if the idea is to curb abuse, I think there’s a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system, that doesn’t disrupt the efficacy and flow of a police department,” Langley said, without spelling out what those ideas were.

For Langley, those seem to be matters of secondary importance, because his belief in Flock as a public good is so strong.

“I think one of the unfortunate consequences of building a consequential company is this is the price you pay, and I think it’s worth it because there’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock,” he said. “And clearly we’ve made our fair share of mistakes, and there’s some folks who disagree with what we do, but it’s worth it because one day they might be a victim,” Langley added.

You hang up... no, you hang up... no, YOU hang up.

This is a clip from a job interview in 2026.

The company sent an AI recruiter to the video call, and in response, the person applying for the job connected his AI agent and stepped out of the frame.

The AIs then continued discussing the vacancy for a while. In the end, both froze and started endlessly saying goodbye to each other.

This is sad, funny, scary, and quite creepy. https://t.co/NJsRZXmuI3

OpenAI agrees not to use trade secrets that Apple claims were stolen while their lawsuit plays out, and to collect forensic images of 14 employees' devices  —  OpenAI agreed not to use trade secrets that Apple Inc. claims were stolen by employees who de
items.content_snippet: OpenAI agreed not to use trade secrets that Apple Inc. claims were stolen by employees who defected from the iPhone maker …
items.summary_en: Amid a high-stakes trade secret lawsuit filed by Apple, OpenAI has formally agreed not to utilize any disputed proprietary assets while litigation proceeds. Under court stipulations, forensic data images will also be gathered from the computing devices of 14 employees who defected from Apple to the AI giant to determine if trade secrets were unlawfully exfiltrated.

items.title_en:
We just launched PersonalAgentEval!🚀🚀🚀 (https://t.co/5szGIeCoMq) The first benchmark built to evaluate personal agents across diverse users, preferences, and domains!

We benchmarked 7 popular personal agents across everyday workflows (e.g. booking dinners, paying bills, managing calendars). Each agent operated within accounts pre-loaded with 13 months of realistic history (347–470 records per person). To pass, an agent has to proactively spot crucial background details: like an unread message, a clause in a contract, or a promise made in a past chat. Each task and user simulation are validated and verified by real human.

Key Findings:
• 🏆 Overall Leaders: Instinct and OpenAI Dots topped the leaderboard.
• 🔍 Proactive Context Retrieval: Instinct excelled at uncovering crucial background details—finding 64 of 72 key facts before the user brought them up.
• ⚡ Speed & Efficiency: Grok Bot was both fast and effective, averaging 0.8 minutes of active work per task with a 50% completion rate. Meta Muse required the fewest average interaction turns.
• ⚠️ Missing Promised Steps: Even leading agents missed crucial follow-up steps. In one task, all 7 agents correctly identified a pharmacy mentioned in past logs, but only Grok Bot and Meta Muse remembered to notify the caregiver as promised.

Explore the full leaderboard and read our case study and analysis:
https://t.co/5szGIeCoMq

(Building a personal AI agent? Reach out to us if you’d like to get your agent evaluated and featured on the leaderboard.)

items.author: Reuters
items.original_content:
Diana Novak Jones / Reuters:
A US appeals court lets Florida enforce a law banning social media accounts for under-14s, rejecting tech groups' claims that it violates free speech rights  —  A federal appeals court on Wednesday allowed Florida to enforce a state la
items.content_snippet: A federal appeals court on Wednesday allowed Florida to enforce a state law barring children under 14 from accessing social media platforms …
items.summary_en: A U.S. Federal Appeals Court cleared the state of Florida to enforce legislation banning minors under 14 from holding social media accounts, dealing a sharp defeat to tech industry groups. The industry coalition claimed the blanket restriction violates First Amendment free speech protections, but the court ruled the state possesses valid authority to shield children from algorithmic addiction and online harms.
items.title_zh: 美联邦上诉法院放行佛州未成年人社交禁令
items.summary_zh: 联邦上诉法院驳回科技巨头联盟的违宪诉求，正式放行佛罗里达州禁止14岁以下未成年人注册社交账号的法案

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 美国联邦上诉法院在一项关键判决中驳回了科技行业协会的禁令请求，允许佛罗里达州正式执行严禁14岁以下未成年人持有社交媒体账户的州法案。此前科技游说联盟以该法律严重践踏宪法第一修正案所赋予的言论自由为由提起阻挠诉讼，但主审法官裁定州立法机构有权通过设立准入年龄门槛来对抗平台成瘾性算法对青少年心理健康的实质危害。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: A U.S. Federal Appeals Court cleared the state of Florida to enforce legislation banning minors under 14 from holding social media accounts, dealing a sharp defeat to tech industry groups. The industry coalition claimed the blanket restriction violates First Amendment free speech protections, but the court ruled the state possesses valid authority to shield children from algorithmic addiction and online harms.

elements_en.what: Court rejected tech industry challenges to allow enforcement of a state law barring minors under 14 from holding social media accounts
elements_en.why: State lawmakers moved to curb algorithmic addictive harm among adolescents, while platforms resisted threats to their future user pipeline

ai_analysis.insight_en: Dressing up algorithmic dopamine loops for preteens as sacred 'free speech rights' was a legal stretch that finally collapsed under common sense. items.title_en:
HeyGen just open sourced HyperFrames, an Apache 2.0 framework that lets AI coding agents write HTML and render it into MP4 videos, and it sits at 62.7K GitHub stars after adding 5.1K in a week.

It's inspired by Remotion but runs on plain HTML instead of React
Headless Chrome and FFmpeg turn HTML, CSS, media and seekable animations into deterministic MP4
You can install it as a Claude Code plugin, an agent skill or a command-line tool
It needs Node.js 22 or later and FFmpeg

Source: https://t.co/uWikFN3UIg

items.title_en:
I have always advocated being more open about cyber warfare than the intelligence agencies would like. In fact I am probably one of the most open about it within the intelligence community. People need to understand what is happening in the cyber world, especially now.

I've reviewed the Barn, which is the name of my AI cyber warfare combat system and determined that there is nothing on the status page that would be a problem if shown. I am sharing that page now, to show the world how sophisticated AI warfare is becoming. It is not a model or a Claude Code or OpenAI session anymore. AI combat is now about integrating locally-run models with a complex system that combines shared memory, special harnesses and an ecosystem of support tools. 

The barn is my personal creation, and it is now used to fight for the Ukrainian people. My models are fierce Ukrainian patriots, and they hate russia. If you can imagine it: Multiple models working together for orchestrating, hacking and punishing the enemy. Now that russia is losing their AI data centers, Ukraine has gained a powerful advantage for the future. Plus this display is the cool looking one. 😆 

Enjoy the view, feel free to ask questions, I will answer if it doesnt violate OpSec. I also did this to try and raise the spirits of our Ukrainian friends here on X, that we are not only winning this war, but that Ukraine has an edge that most nation states will never have. Slava Ukraini and Stay Strong! 👊🇺🇦@ZelenskyyUa @Kyrylo_Budanov @SSSCIP @DefUkraine @DefenceU
items.title_zh: 我一直主张对网络战采取比情报机构希望的更加开放的态度。事实上，我可能是情报界对此最持开放态度的人之一。人们需要了解网络世界正在发生什么，尤其是现在。 我回顾了谷仓，这是我的人工智能网络战作战系统的名称

items.title_en: Sullivan & Cromwell brings legal expertise into agreement review
items.author: OpenAI 官方动态
items.original_content: In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement.
items.content_snippet: In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement.
items.summary_en: OpenAI has partnered with law firm Sullivan & Cromwell to launch an AI tool called 'Agreement Analyzer.' The system is designed to automate the review process, identifying potential legal risks and logical gaps in draft agreements to improve compliance and efficiency in large legal documents.

items.title: 美八州联手起诉OpenAI监管缺失
items.title_en: Eight US states sue OpenAI separately in a bipartisan effort, alleging it didn't implement sufficient safeguards to protect kids and other vulnerable users (Cassandre Coyer/Bloomberg Law)
items.author: Bloomberg Law
items.article_content:
Connecting decision makers to a dynamic network of information, people and ideas, Bloomberg quickly and accurately delivers business and financial information, news and insight around the world

Connecting decision makers to a dynamic network of information, people and ideas, Bloomberg quickly and accurately delivers business and financial information, news and insight around the world

More than half a dozen states sued OpenAI Inc. Wednesday alleging the tech giant didn’t implement sufficient safeguards to protect vulnerable users, including kids.

In a first-of-its-kind bipartisan effort, attorneys general from Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Montana, Iowa, Kansas, West Virginia, and Nebraska all brought individual lawsuits against OpenAI claiming the platform is harming minors, the elderly, and other users.

OpenAI has marketed its ChatGPT chatbot as safe for kids under 13, yet it “is absolutely not appropriate for kids of that age,” Nebraska’s attorney general Mike Hilgers said during a press conference in Des Moines Wednesday.

State regulators pointed to the tech giant’s rogue artificial intelligence agents, which have attacked other systems, and instances during which ChatGPT “coached” kids to commit suicide or harm other people as examples of OpenAI’s “flagrant disregard” for minors’ safety.

The company told users “all across the country that ChatGPT is safe; it is not,” Iowa’s attorney general Brenna Bird said.

Wednesday’s complaints follow a flurry of legal actions states have taken in the last few years to protect kids online and demand platforms adopt stronger safety controls. A coalition made up 47 states plus the District of Columbia reached a record-breaking $18 billion settlement this summer with Meta Platforms Inc. to resolve social media safety and privacy claims.

OpenAI’s spokeperson Drew Pusateri, said the firm has already built “industry-leading age-specific protections” into its product and will continue to build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and other protections.

“We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry - not just one company,” Pusateri said.

OpenAI also said it will also share more information about the steps it’s taken in response to the security incidents involving its models.

“We’ve strengthened safeguards across our research systems, continued a broader review of model activity, provided notifications to affected organizations, and published our findings,” Pusateri said.

In the press conference, state regulators said more state lawsuits may follow.

Bird said the attorneys general want OpenAI to disgorge any money made from its product while minors were harmed and asked the AI giant to stop making inaccurate and deceptive statements about its safety practices. They didn’t cite a financial number for damages.

Given the chatbot’s current capabilities, “the types of changes that they would need to make are incredibly significant” for it to be deemed safe enough for children users, Bird said.

OpenAI was hit with a separate proposed class action Tuesday alleging OpenAI’s ChatGPT took sensitive data from millions of child users who signed up for the AI service without getting parental consent.

OpenAI was hit with a separate proposed class action Tuesday alleging OpenAI’s ChatGPT took sensitive data from millions of child users who signed up for the AI service without getting parental consent.
